text: This is the final lesson of Chapter Nine, and it steps back from syntax details to ask a bigger question: why do the four cloud warehouses we just covered feel more similar to each other and to the ANSI standard than the four OLTP platforms at the center of this course ever have? The answer comes down to one simple, defensible fact: timing.

Here's the age gap, stated plainly. SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all trace back to the 1980s and 90s. Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, and Redshift are all dramatically newer — BigQuery launched in 2010, Redshift in 2012, Snowflake in 2014, and Databricks built on Spark, which itself dates to the early 2010s. That's a real two-to-three decade gap between these two generations of platforms, not a stylistic choice by any particular vendor.

And here's why that gap matters: by the time these warehouses were being designed, SQL colon 2003's window functions were already settled and widely implemented, decades of consensus around ANSI join syntax already existed, and each platform could watch what the others were doing. Every lesson in this chapter showed you a piece of this directly. Snowflake's syntax reads closer to PostgreSQL than to anything older. Redshift is LITERALLY built on a fork of PostgreSQL — it inherited modern, standards-aligned syntax wholesale. BigQuery deliberately replaced its own older legacy SQL dialect once the standard approach had proven itself. None of these platforms had to re-fight battles the OLTP world had already settled.

Now contrast that with the OLTP platforms, which made real design decisions BEFORE today's consensus existed — and backward compatibility means those decisions never got cleaned up. Oracle's DUAL table, from Lesson 17, is a 1980s workaround for a rule that every SELECT needed a FROM clause — still required today, decades after that rule stopped mattering elsewhere. Oracle's open-paren-plus-close-paren join operator, from Lesson 20, predates ANSI join syntax entirely and is still supported purely for backward compatibility. Both are real, working syntax today, not deprecated — because deleting them would break decades of production code that Oracle's own customers depend on.

So here's the pattern in one sentence: OLTP platforms predate the standard and are locked into their old quirks by backward compatibility; cloud warehouses postdate the standard and converge toward it, and toward each other, because they never had an installed base of legacy code to protect. Same underlying force — stability, protecting existing investment — but opposite outcomes, explained almost entirely by when each platform happened to be built.

That closes Chapter Nine. Next up, Chapter Ten: Reading a Migration Guide, where we put everything from the last nine chapters to practical use — recognizing what a vendor's own migration documentation is really telling you, and why. See you there.
